Lewis was arrested and jailed. Lewis is a colored restaurant keeper who keeps a restaurant at Barnum. SHAKEN UP AGAIN.

The Fourth street rock cut, which; two weeks ago, was the scene of a harrowing dynamite accident, by which seven men lost their lives, was again brought prominently before the city this afternoon by another explosion of dynamite, which, though no lives were lost, was more destructive to property than the former explosion. About 4 o'clock the blast was exploded in the usual way, but the concussion was so great that seventy-five pounds of dynamite stored only 100 feet away for further use, went into the air with startling results. About thirty houses in the immediate vicinity of the explosion were more or less damaged, windows broken, doors torn from their hinges, pictures and clocks shaken from the walls and six blocks away, in the Hotel St. Louis building and opera house block, large panes of glass were shattered as though hit by flying rocks. Women and children rushed from their houses, panic stricken, and, strangely enough, although several people were thrown down on the streets no one was hurt. The damage to houses is estimated at $3,000. Contractor Fitzpatrick says the dynamite which exploded was just about to be used in blasting.

Albert Lewis, Accused of Murder, Now in Jail.
THE HISTORY OF THE CRIME.
Something About the West Superior Plant---Notes Gathered Here and There.
Special to the Globe.
DULUTH March 21
DULUTH, March 21.—Albert Lewis, of Barnum, who is accused of killing Frank Burke, a stranger, on the 12th of March, is now at the county jail. Lewis is an inoffensive-looking mulatto, apparently about forty years of age. He made his home in Duluth from 1865 to 1885, being engaged at the Windsor hotel and later at the Merchants. He was also in business for himself. Lewis claims Burke came to his place for a room, and that he told him he had none. Burke insisted on getting a room, became violent, attacked him, and, in self defense, he raised a pine stick and struck Burke several times with it. He did not think Burke could have been fatally injured by these blows. He thinks Burke fell and received more severe injuries after leaving the place. Burke was a section hand on the St. Paul & Duluth road, and no relatives have yet turned up to claim the body.

Manager Wemyss, of the West Superior Land and River Improvement company, with engineers of the company, has been prospecting for two days to locate the new steel plant of the company at West Superior. People about West Superior and Duluth have at last stopped all conjecture in regard to the plant and take it as an accepted and very satisfactory fact. Manager Wemyss states that $1,500,000 has been subscribed to build the works, and $1,000,000 additional has been subscribed for working capital. Of this amount the Land and River company took $500,000. In about ten days the names of the directors and officers, who are mostly New York men, will be given to the public. There are thirty men now employed on the foundation to the new hotel at West Superior, and at a meeting of the chamber or commerce yesterday a committee of three was appointed to confer with the pail and tub factory people with reference to the establishment of a pail and tub factory on the other side of the bay.

The Ropes Were Around Their Necks.
Globe-Democrat: For several months past the stockmen owning cattle in the southern part of De Soto county, south Florida, have been suffering from the depredations of a well-organized band of cow thieves, who make their headquarters in Lee county, nearly opposite Fort Myers. The marks and brands of hundreds of beef cattle were changed and then driven to Myers and Punta Rassa, where they were sold to parties buying for the Key West market. The eattlemen received information from parties in Myers that cattle with bloody ears and poorly disguised brands were being brought to that market for sale by the Corbett brothers, who, it seems, were the leaders in this wholesale steal.

Recently a body of the principal stock owners of DeSoto county surprised the Corbetts at their home before daybreak, and demanded an explanation of the charges that had been brought against them. They refused to give any satisfaction and seized their guns, mounted their horses and attempted to leave, but were brought to bay by the Winchesters of the stockmen. Several shots were fired before they would yield, but at last they surrendered. Ropes were placed around the necks of the three Corbetts, and the enraged cattlemen were for at once pulling them over the limb of a convenient water oak. One was actually pulled off of the ground, when his struggles awoke some pity and calmer counsels prevailed. With the stout ropes around their necks the Corbetts confessed that they had just returned from Fort Myers, where they had disposed of hundreds of head of stolen cattle. The cattlemen give them the alternative of leaving the country within ten days or hanging. They begged for a longer time, but it being refused they promised to leave. The stockmen are determined to put a stop to this nefarious business, and it will go hard with these men if they do not leave in the time allowed them, as the cattlemen's word here is the only law that is respected.

FURTHER PARTICULARS OF THE TACKETT'S MILLS AFFAIR. How It Originated—Knives, Pistols, and Weights—Fires—A Distressing Powder-Horn Accident.
FREDERICKSBURG, VA., December 28.—The latest reports your correspondent can get from the riot which occurred at Tackett's Mills, in Stafford county, last Wednesday show that there were a number engaged in it and that it originated between the three Heflin brothers—Messrs. Warren, Benton, and Thomas—and two negroes named Henry Brown and George Black. After the fracas began a number of both races joined in and a general riot ensued. The difficulty seems to have grown out of an old grudge and politics combined. On the morning the row took place a large number of blacks and whites had assembled in the store of Mr. L. K. Skinner, at that place, to enjoy Christmas, and after conversing for some time on different topics in a friendly manner politics were taken up and in a short while aroused all hands to fever-heat. Some words then passed between Mr. Benton Heflin and the negro Henry Brown, which resulted in Brown being knocked down by Mr. Heflin, who commenced to bent him while he was lying on the floor. A general fight then took place, and all parties present became engaged in it. During the melee the negro Geo. Black drew his revolver and fired at Mr. Heflin, missing him. Knives, pistols, and weights were then brought into use by both parties, during which the negro Black shot Mr. Benton Heflin in the left side, the ball entering the heart, killing him instantly. Black then escaped, but was pursued and is reported captured and lodged in the county jail. Brown has since died from the effects of his injuries and several others are reported painfully injured. Mr. Heflin was married and leaves a wife and two children.

At this writing considerable excitement still prevails, and a renewal of the fight at any time would not be surprising. The Commonwealth's Attorney and the officers of the county are doing their best to maintain order, and all parties connected with the affair are being arrested.

A distressing accident occurred near Robey's crossing, on the P., F. & P. K. R., in this county, on last Wednesday evening which will probably result fatally to two parties. William Pryor and wife (colored), who live at the crossing, left their home in the morning to visit some neighbors, leaving their six children at home. The eidest, being sixteen years old, started off for the woods and had only been absent a few minutes when he heard a deafening noise and screams. Hurrying to the house he discovered the children in the yard, four of whom were writting in agony. The children, it seems, after their brother had left desired to have some fun in shooting fire crackers, and they not making the noise they desired got their father's powder-horn and, going out into the yard, built a fire and gathered around it. Mary, aged twelve, threw the powder-horn on the coals, when an instantaneous explosion followed, driving the blaze full into their faces and burning them all except the youngest in such a manner that the skin fell from them.

SALIDA, Colo., August 28.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—Information has reached there that Pap Ryland, who owned a ranch on the Sweet Water and was a character in western Colorado, died at his ranch last evening from a bullet wound, inflicted by C. A. Babcock of whom very little is known except that he is a large man, about thirty-five years old. Babcock, went to Glenwood Springs and surrendered himself to Deputy Sheriff Little. He claims he shot Ryland in self-defense, but his stories about the affair are very conflicting as to detail. Babcock mounted a horse, rode to Doterso and caught the train for Glenwood Springs in the nick of time to save being lynched by Ryland's neighbors. James M. Ryland, a son of the murdered man, is a journalist and is at present connected with the Ute Chief at Glenwood Springs.

Pap Ryland's ranch has for many years been a land mark and stopping place for travelers and hunters and his hospitality was proverbial. He was the last remnant of the white men who had the temerity to pitch their tents on the hunting grounds of the Utes when this was their undisputed territory. He was of an irascible temperament, but it is very much doubted whether he attempted the life of Babcock.

PAP RILAND SHOT.
The Murderer Mounts a Horse and Escapes Being Lynched.
[SPECIAL TO THE EVENING WORLD.]

DENVER, Col., Aug. 29.—Early Monday morning Pap Riland was shot at his ranch on Sweetwater Creek by C. A. Babcock. He died last evening from the effects of his wounds. Pat Riland was one of the characters of Western Colorado. His ranch on the Sweetwater was the first located in this section.

In the early days of California Gulch Pap Riland was among the proprietors. Twenty-five years ago he was one of the pioneers of Summit County. Hardly a mining camp in that part of the State has enjoyed even a temporary boom but he hastened to the scene, eager to be among the first to win the imaginary bonanza prize.

This is another added to the long list of mysterious tragedies of which the isolated mountains of Colorado have been the sole and dumb witness. Babcock and Pap were alone when it occurred. He left him right after the shooting, came down from the ranch to Dotsero, a distance of sixteen miles, and took a train for Glenwood Springs, where he gave himself up to Deputy Sheriff Little. The story he tells is that he was forced to shoot his aged victim in self-defense. His narration was confused and distorted.

As soon as the ranchers on the Sweetwater were made aware of the tragedy they were greatly incensed. As they collected together they began to talk freely of lynching Babcock. While they were considering the matter and preparing to act a friend of Babcock managed to get to one side and mounted him on a horse, and he thus got away and arrived at Dotsero in the nick of time to catch the morning train for Glenwood.

A Little Girl Brutally Assaulted.
NOVILLE. Tenn. July. 1
KNOXVILLE, Tenn., July 18.—A most horrible outrage was committed upon a twelve-year-old girl last night, within 200 yards of the corporation limits. Frances Robinson, the daughter of a poor washerwoman, living in the eastern part of the city, was returning from a suburban residence, where she had gone to deliver a bundle of clothes. It was shortly after dark, and as the girl neared the city limits an unknown white man accosted her very pleasantly and offered to escort her home. They walked on for some distance, and when opposite a corn field the villian seized her, dragged her over a wire fence into the standing corn and outraged her. It was several hours before she reached home, and the facts of the outrage were not known to any one but the police until after midnight. The girl was perhaps fatally injured. The demon had used a knife to accomplish his purpose. She gave the police a description of her assailant, William Carter, alias Clark, was arrested at his home about 1 o'clock this morning. His clothes were covered with blood, and a colored man identified him as the person seen walking with the girl before the outrage was committed. Clark was taken before his victim this afternoon and she identified him. He was lodged in jail. There is considerable talk of lynching. This is the third outrage on children committed in this city and suburbs within the last week. and all by white men.

STRONG TALK OF LYNCHING. William Amrine, a Switchman, Maltreated and Murdered by a Saloonist at Ashland.
Saloonist at Ashland.

ASHLAND, Wis., Aug. 29.—At 3 o'clock this morning, William Amrine, a switchman in the employ of the Wisconsin Central road, was shot and killed by Dan Ritchie, a saloonkeeper, in front of his place in the "Bay City" district. The men had a misunderstanding while intoxicated, and Ritchie knocked Amrine down and stamped on his face with his boots, taking him into a back room to administer this brutal punishment. Two policemen were present, and they separated the men, putting Amrine out on the street, when he grabbed a handful of gravel and threw it through the window. Ritchie then grabbed a revolver and ran out, and before the officers could stop him, he emptied five chambers of his gun at the retreating form of Amrine, two of which took effect, one in the back of the head and another in the hip. The coroner's jury found a verdict in accordance with the facts, and Ritchie is in jail. There was some strong talk during the day among railroad men, who were in favor of lynching. Extra precautions will be taken to-night to prevent anything of the kind. Amrine leaves a widowed monther at Bloomington, Ill.

Monticello, May 25.—Chamberlain, the murderer of Ida Wittenberg, and Catterson, one of the tramps who escaped jail after assaulting the sheriff, last night, are still at large. Hundreds of citizens are scouring the country in all directions searching for them, and it is reported that the searchers are close upon the trail, and will probably bag their game to-night. Benson, the younger of the tramps, was brought in at noon and has given valuable information as to the direction taken by the two yet at large. Should they be captured it is not probable that lynching will be resorted to, although it would have been probably different last night. The sheriff has one arm broken and his skull is fractured. The Board of Commissioners have offered $800 reward for the capture of Chamberlain and $200 for Catterson.

Chamberlain's crime was peculiarly shocking. He was in love with a beautiful and attractive young lady named Ida Wittenberg, a daughter of a wealthy and highly respected family living at Reynolds, in White county. He claims that Miss Wittenberg had promised to marry him, but afterwards, tiring of him, had accepted the attentions of another suitor. On the night of the murder Miss Wittenberg had been to church, in company with the favored suitor. Chamberlain placed himself in ambush near her home, and awaited her return. Her escort left her at the gate, and she proceeded to a door at the rear of the house to gain admission. Here she was attacked by Chamberlain, who attempted to overpower her, but she resisted him successfully until he placed a revolver at her mouth and fired. The girl fell to the ground helpless, but the report of the revolver and her cries for help had reached the ears of her escort, who returned in time to find Chamberlain retreating from the scene of his crime. The murderer, as he retreated, fired three shots at his rival. Miss Wittenberg suffered severely for ten days and died. During this time Chamberlain was under heavy bail. After the death of his victim he was placed in jail, and for safe keeping was taken first to Delphi and then Lafayette. He was returned to Monticello two weeks ago for trial, which was postponed to the September term.

How Chamberlain Was Captured.

CHICAGO, May 26.—A special to the Times from Monticello, Ind., says: "To two young ladies, cousins of Chamberlain, is due the credit of the capture of the desperado, and the coolness and judgment they displayed in the matter made them the heroines of the hour. Last evening, an hour before sundown, Chamberlain entered the house of his uncle, William Biddle, six miles from Reynolds. Biddle is a widower, and was away from home. His daughters, Ida and May, aged nineteen and twenty-one, keep house for him. Their feelings can hardly be described as they stood face to face with the young man, who was almost as near to them as a brother, with whom they had been raised, and who at that moment was being hunted by a thousand armed men. Chamberlain was almost exhausted. For the entire night and day he had dodged about the country in the rain, without a bite to eat or a moment to rest. He was the picture of despair. His first question was as to whether the officers had been at the house searching for him. When informed that a deputy sheriff had searched the house but an hour before, he dropped on a sofa for a short rest. His cousins induced him to remove his clothing and hang them to the fire to dry. The moment he fell asleep they searched the garments thoroughly, but found no weapons. They at once decided to turn him over to the authorities, and, while Ida remained at the house, Mary ran across the fields and told her story to Ralph and Arthur Laurie, their nearest neighbors. Armed with shotguns and accompanied by Charles Eckert and Jacob Fisher, the five young men approached the house. There they removed their boots, and, headed by Arthur Laurie, they quietly opened the door to the room in which Chamberlain was lying. Lourie drew a bead on the desperado, and in a second the other four had sprung upon him and bound him. He was taken completely by surprise. It was midnight before arrangements were made to start for this place. The parting between Chamberlain and his cousins was touching. The prisoner breaking down and giving the first evidence of feeling he has exhibited since the cruel murder of his sweetheart, six weeks ago.

"Company A, of the First Regiment of State troops, arrived in Monticello this afternoon, under orders from Governor Gray, to prevent a lynching. The presence of the troops only had the effect of increasing the excitement and further enraging the people."

Monticello, May 26.—[Special.]—Cham. berlain was captured last evening at 9 p. m. at the home of his uncle, William Biddle, two miles from his father's home, while laying asleep upon the lounge. His captors were Jacob Fisher, Arthur and Ralph Lawrie and a man named Eggert. They were neighbors, and were informed of his presence by his cousin, Miss Mary Biddle. He was overpowered before being able to offer any resistance, securely bound and brought to Monticello at 3 o'clock this morning. The news of his capture spread over the country like wildfire, and by 9 o'clock the town was filled with people. While there were individual expressions in favor of lynching, the better sense of the people appeared to prevail, and no immediate danger seemed to threaten until the arrival of the 3 p. m. train from the south when, without notice, there filed therefrom a company of state militia from Delphi under command of Capt. Edward Gresham, which proceeded to and immediately surrounded the jail with a guard, relieving the civil officers. Upon investigation it was found that Judge Gould had telegraphed to Gov. Gray for a company of the state militia and that this company had come in response to the governor's order. The people feeling that there was no immediate danger and that the citizens with the assistance of the civil officers of White county were willing and able to prevent any outbreak on the part of a mob, became exasperated, and great excitement has prevailed ever since. Frequent threats of lynching have been indulged and all evening people from remote towns and parts of the country have been flocking in until 1,500 persons are now in town. The guard has been withdrawn from the outside and the company now stationed within the jail. While I write the soldiers are loading their guns preparatory to repelling any attack that may be made upon the jail. Judge Gould is receiving his share of censure for this apparent premature coming in of troops, especially from Delphi, the scene of the Amer Green lynching. Three Prisoners in the White County(Ind.) Jail Make a Deadly Assault on the Sheriff and Escape — A Lynching in Prospect When They Are Captured.

DELPHI, Ind., May 25.—Monticello, in the adjoining county of White, is wrought up to a high pitch of excitement. Three prisoners, Ed Chamberlain, Albert Benson and Robert Catterson, assaulted Sheriff Joseph Henderson and escaped. Shortly after eight o'clock last night the sheriff went into the corridor to lock the prisoners up in their cells. Chamberlain brained him with an iron bar, and all three rushed into the jail office, smashed a window and jumped to liberty. The sheriff's skull was fractured and one arm broken. His injuries are fatal. Chamberlain is under indictment for the murder of Ella Wittenberg, his sweetheart, at Reynolds, six weeks ago. To escape a mob he was removed to this city and then to Lafayette. After the excitement swept over he was taken back to White County, and there was a determination to give him a fair trial. Benson and Catterson were tramps awaiting trial for highway robbery. Both have served time in Michigan City penitentiary. Before leaving all three wrote long letters. Chamberlain stated that the unwholesome atmosphere of the jail was undermining his health; that this was his only chance for his life; that he had done right in murdering his sweetheart, and would advise others in similar situations to do the same thing. The tramps stated that they recognized that there was no chance for them to get justice in Indiana.

The whole country for miles around is aroused. It is not thought that Chamberlain can possibly escape. He took a western course, and the hunt is in that direction. If captured it is the general opinion that he will never return to Monticello alive. In his letter he stated that he would die rather than return to jail.

The sheriff entered the jail with a cocked revolver, but was completely trapped. His wife witnessed the entire affair and gave the alarm. The streets were lined with people when the escape was made, and a number saw the flying fugitives.

The following reprints from THE APPEAL of 1869 are made in continuation of the history of Arkansas, which appeared in THE APPEAL on Sunday morning. These additional proofs will serve to show the desperate lengths to which Gov. Powell Clayton went in the mal-administration of the State's affairs.

THE FULTON COUNTY MURDERS.

January 6.—The signal cause of the outrages (the Fulton county murders] seems to have been an old grudge, originating long before the war, between one Simpson Mason, a shoe maker, and a family of Martins. * * * The first shedding of blood occurred in the spring of 1864, when a party of men, alleged to have been led by Mason, took James Martin and his son from their home and deliberately shot them down. * * * A few days later Frank Martin was taken from his home at the head of Polk bayou, in Independence county, conducted about half a mile into the woods and shot down in the same manner. On the 11th of June, 1865, subsequent to the surrender, a party of twenty men, led by Mason, killed in a similar manner Sam Payne and John Hallingsworth. * * * In September last Simpson Mason was himself shot down while passing along the road by unknown parties. Soon after this the sheriff of Fulton county made several arrests, and a desperado named Monks from across the Missouri line—Fulton county joins Missouri—made his appearance so suddenly with a gang of men as to induce the belief of preconcerted action. Monks, under pretense of assisting the sheriff in the enforcement of of the law took possession of the prisoners, but released them on a writ of habeas corpus issued from the circuit court of that county, Judge Baxter presiding. One of them, Uriah B. Bush fared, unfortunately. He was delivered to Deputy Sheriff Turner after dark and shot down by a party of men in disguise who are believed on the strongest evidence to have been a portion of Monks' band.

Monks then retired across the Missouri borders too late for a posse of about 300 citizens, who gathered and offered their services as a posse to reach him, if, indeed, the sheriff would have consented to avail himself of their services at all. It is believed, of course, that he would not, but a plausable excuse must suffice for a test of the question, and the sheriff is welcome to its benefit. Thus matters rested until the 22d of November, when one Col. Dale suddenly made his appearance with about 100 militia gathered up in Fulton and adjacent counties, and a few days later he was joined by Monks with a band of from ten to twenty-five Missourians. This force made its headquarters at Talbert's mill, in the northwestern portion of Fulton county, and after quieting apprehensions in some measure by treating the citizens fairly, they suddenly commenced a raid upon the people of a character seldom, if ever, outdone in time of war. Squads of from ten to twenty or thirty scouted the country far and near, taking horses, clothing, provisions of every sort, robbing and stealing and plundering generally. Necessity does not seem to have limited the unlawful acts of these desperate men. The waste caused will doubtless far exceed what was required and the terrorism spread far and near, resulting in a great portion of the citizens leaving their homes, neglecting their crops and business. On the 13th we learn from private communication they were still there; thus for nearly a month 130 or 140 men, as we are informed, half fed and half clad, having supplied their wants in the way of food, clothing and horses and have plundered and robbed indiscriminately to satisfy cupidity and private revenge. Where acts like these are to end none can tell. Thus far the sufferers in this revengeful works of blood and carnage have been "rebels" with the single exception of Simpson Mason, who claimed to be a Union man, and who committed his bloody acts under that cloak.

THE "ROGUES' MARCH."

January 17.—Five hundred and fifty of Clayton's melish called in from the southwest to be paid off (in depreciated State scrip) and were marched through Little Rock by the thirty or forty carpetbaggers, who constitute what is called the Governor's guard, of Little Rock, preceded by a United States garrison band, playing the well known "Rogues' march." I suppose since, that would have been the most appropriate musical composition with which to have welcomed them. Mounted on steeds in a procession of two and two, which Rosa Bonheur could not have witnessed without convulsions, hard-checked men and boys, decorated about their persons with streamers of red flannel, with Brigadier-General Calterson and staff, at their head, all with hats bound with red flannel captured from the enemy, doubtless, preceded by Clayton, they fled through the principal streets, making a show of power at the command of the usurping Governor, whose thoughts are those that have taken possession of all tyrants from time immemorial.

PLUNDERING AS THEY GO.

January 18—We learn from passengers down the river that Gen. Upham, in command of about 150 cavalry militia, passed Cotton Point on their way to Osceola on Friday evening. They are represented as plundering as they go along, and families are removing themselves, with everything removable, across the river. The trading boats along the river have also quit the Arkansas shore and have gone to the Tennessee side.
TORTURE AND MURDER OF PRISONERS.
January 19.—News from Marion gives particulars of the lawless, murderous and infamous proceedings of the mob called militia. Five citizens have been held in jail at Marion, charged with various crimes by the militia, who promised to give these prisoners a fair trial. All these pledged and promises, made but to lull into fancied
george-wallace-marion-1888-01-21.A3:
security the prisoners and their friends, have been broken—basely, faithlessly and ruthlessly broken—and on Saturday three of the unfortunates were taken from the jail, carried to Frenche's bayou and shot to death. Previous to executing them, the fiends tied their arms behind their backs and throwing the rope over the limb of a tree, repeatedly raised and lowered them, causing unspeakable agony, but failing to elicit one word of self-condemnation from them—the object of the torture. The names of two of the unfortunates were Harney (said to be a nephew of Gen. Harney) and Skipp. The other we could not learn. Our informant states that no women are allowed to leave the county. This fact, in view of the late proceedings of the militia, is extremely suggestive, and ought to, of itself, be enough to rouse the men throughout the country to instant action. After shooting the three men a portion of the militia went on to Osceola. The names of the men shot were George L. Harney, William Ticer and A. McAllister.

ANOTHER MURDER.

January 21.—We learn that Dr. John R. Acree, well known in opr city, was shot and killed on Monday by the band who shot Messrs. Harney, Ticer and McAllister. He saw them coming and knowing that he was obnoxious to them tried to escape, but was overtaken and killed.

TORTURING THE PRISONERS.

January 22—Parties both white and negro, radical and conservative, have assured us that for days before the three unfortunate men were taken out and murdered all five of the prisoners in the Marion jail were tortured in the most awful and inhuman manner and forced to make confessions. Wofford, who now remains in the jail and likely to suffer the same fate as his three comrades, was tortured more than the others. They were tied up by the thumbs for hours, their elbows were drawn together and tied behind their backs, and in this position they would be swung up to a limb with weights fastened to their feet, and kept thus until their arms were nearly torn from their sockets. Ropes were twisted tightly around their necks until life was nearly extinct, their faces were black and their tongues, black and swollen, protruded two inches out of their mouths. Mr. Wofford, after being thus choked, was with difficulty resuscitated. The four negro militiamen—Bill Porter, Monroe Allen, Wm. Reese and Hector Allen, who were convicted of raping two white ladies, by a court-martial composed mostly of negroes, were executed on Tuesday, a short distance beyond the barricades. The condemned men pleaded guilty, and pleaded and prayed for life in the most agonizing manner. The ladies were permitted and are leaving the country and coming to Memphis.

MORE KILLING.

January 25.—We learn of the murder on Saturday of George Wallace, a young man well known in Memphis and a resident of the neighborhood of Mound City. When Clayton's bandits first came to Marion he fled to Memphis and remained here several days. On Friday, hearing that his mother, whose sole stay and support he was, was in need, he went over to carry her some provisions. While going with them to his house he met a squad of militia, and fearing harm turned and fled. They pursued, fired upon and killed him instantly.

A Threat From Sambalino.

Adolf Sambalino, who was extradited from Antwerp for forgeries committed while he was employed by David Spero, a feather merchant, pleaded not guilty yesterday and Recorder Smyth sent him to the Tombs in default of $10,000 bail. Sambalino said that he had committed his forgeries to shield others and that somebody would be astonished when his trial came on.

Herr von Levetzow, Conservative, was elected President of the Reichstag yesterday.

Signor Ingami, a Roman advocate who died recently, left 1,000,000 francs to the Pope.

Adam Berkes of Sardinia, Ohio, who was flogged by masked men last Saturday night, has become insane.

The Fort Wayne Jenney Electric Light Company's plant was destroyed by fire yesterday. The loss on the building and machinery is $250,000.

Chairman Quay has called a meeting of the Executive Committee of the Republican National Committee for Wednesday, Dec. 5, in Washington.

A fire in Pocomoke City, Md., on Thursday destroyed the entire business portion of the town, only two stores remaining. Loss estimated at $500,000.

A fire that started in a dentist's office at Eureka Springs. Ark., yesterday, destroyed the greater part of the business portion of the town. The loss is $200,000.

Fairlawn, a bay colt 2 years old, by Nutwood, dam StreamSet, by Almont, has been sold by Gen. W. T. Withers's Fairlawn stock farm, near Lexington, to G. Lynch, Philadelphia, Pa., for $1,000.

The Connecticut River Railroad station at Chicopee was broken into yesterday morning, during the temporary absence of the depot master, and about $60 or $70 was stolen. The safe was unlocked, but its contents were not disturbed.

John Jones, a negro, who at King's Creek, Tenn., assaulted Mrs. John Haggard and Miss Hedgecath after the ladies had fed him, was pursued by a crowd of angry men, who captured him. It is more than probable that they hanged him.

The Norwegian ship Magnhild, Cant. Tellefsen, from New York Oct. 30, which arrived at Amsterdam Nov. 22, had on board the crew of the Norwegian bark Gibaltar, Capt. Frodersen, which was abandoned, waterlogged, in latitude 45° N. longitude 28° W.

Burglaries broke into the Boston and Maine station at Pine Point, Me., on Thursday night, and blew open the safe. The front windows were shattered by the explosion, and the safe door was blown across the office, demolishing a partition. Thursday was the weekly pay day for the Boston and Maine employees, and the wages of the station men and section hands were in the safe.

The statement published yesterday that Silas Gurney, proprietor of the Tremont House, Boston, had gone into insolvency is incorrect. Mr. Gurney is not the proprietor of the Tremont House, and has not been connected with that hotel since a year ago last January. The proprietors of the Tremont House, H. M. J. J. Barrey, of Vicksburg, Miss., recently sank a gas well at Lake Providence, La. The pressure is good, and the gas burns brilliantly. It is believed the gas field is extensive.

The cotton crop in West Tennessee is yielding much better than was expected a month ago. The staple is larger and better than has been known for years. The streets of Jackson are crowded with cotton bales from morning until night. The outlook for a big holiday trade was never better.

The yellow-fever scourge has entirely abated at Decatur, Ala.

John Peterson, wanted in Ashville, N. C., for murder, has been captured in Blout County, Tenn.

An unsuccessful attempt was made a few nights ago, to burn the building occupied by the Birmingham (Ala.) Age-Herald.

Ben Harrison, a colored man of Hopkinsville, Ky., had a fit while driving a wagon, a few days since, and, falling to the ground, broke his neck, dying instantly.

John White, a young farmer living near Hopkinsville, Ky., fell from a loaded wagon, a few evenings since, and broke his back, and received other serious injuries that rendered his recovery doubtful.

Dr. J. I. Walker, a well-known and eccentric citizen of Hopkinsville, Ky., died suddenly a few days since. He recently had a stroke of paralysis, and never rallied. He was a bachelor.

The Garfield Club, of Knoxville, Tenn., composed entirely of white citizens, have made arrangements to attend the inauguration of President Harrison in a body. Two hundred members will go, each wearing a silk hat and overcoat of the same color.

The house of Jack Gregg at Leesville, Ky., was burned a few nights ago, and all the family, consisting of five persons, perished, except Gregg, who was away from the house on business.

While boring for gas in Livingston County, Ky., twelve miles from Paducah, recently, a vein of silver ore was struck at a depth of about eight hundred feet. The vein is said to be about three feet thick, and considerable excitement prevails over the find.

Henry James, colored, and his wife went to a church supper at Livingstone, Ala., a few nights ago, leaving their three children locked up in the house. Upon their return they found the house in ashes, and the children burned to a crisp.

John Peterson, wanted for murder at Asheville, N. C., was arrested in the mountains of Blount County, Tenn., a few days ago, by Deputy Sheriff Blankenship. Peterson killed a man named Gooch last July, the murder being the most horrible ever known in Western North Carolina.

F. H. Varnado, a prominent merchant of Tsyka, Miss., was shot down and instantly killed, a few nights ago. There were no witnesses to the killing, and the assassin is unknown.

O. F. Adams, city treasurer of Macon, Ga., is reported as being about $20,000 short in his accounts, and has been suspended from office. He can give no satisfactory explanation. Demands have been made on his bondsmen.

Some new coal discoveries that have been made near Fordsville, Ky., on the line of the Owensboro & Falls of Rough railroad, hold out better promises than any of the veins yet known in that region.

Jas. Philbeck, a farmer living in Cleveland County, N. C., was called to the door of his house a few nights ago and shot dead by an unknown party, who then entered the premises, shot Philbeck's wife and robbed the house. The murderer escaped.

Robert H. Hailey, of Jackson, Tenn., brakeman on the Mobile & Ohio railroad, fell under the wheels while coupling cars at Guntown, Miss., a few nights ago. The cars passed over his left hand, mangling it in a fearful manner. The unfortunate man was taken to Jackson, where four of his fingers were amputated.

Jack Jones, a negro hailing from Macon, Ga., made an unsuccessful criminal assault on Mrs. John Haggard and Miss Hedgroth, who live near Rockwood, Tenn., a few nights ago. He was afterward caught by an angry mob and lynched.

The recent disappearance of Colonel J. F. Hill, from Morgan County, Ga., has been given additional interest by the disclosures of his wife. She says that three months ago he claimed to have had a vision in which he was ordered to divide up his property and go into a distant land where he was not known. He reached home one night from a neighboring town, and handed his wife the deed for $10,000 worth of property, keeping $5,000 in cash for himself. CHARGED WITH MURDER.
James Erickson, of Cokato, Released on Big Bail.
James Erickson, who murdered John Anderson at Cokato, Oct. 6, was in the district court yesterday morning, to have his bonds fixed. Six well-known citizens stood ready to go bail for him. They were accepted, and Erickson was set at liberty. The trial will take place at Wright county, in December, and Mr. Erwin is expected to spring some unique defense to clear the burly murderer. Erickson was drunk and very pugnacious when he committed the deed. Anderson was a farmer unknown to him, who was talking to a friend in the saloon on the evening in question. Erickson walked up and ordered him with an oath to shut up. He then struck Anderson two heavy blows. The second was in the pit of the stomach and caused the heart instantly to cease beating. Anderson fell a corpse before his now sobered and terrified assailant. He left a family without means of support. Erickson barely escaped lynching at the time.

Ole C. Olson, who was school treasurer of Wolsey township, Dakota, got deeply into debt via chattle mortgages, and, it is claimed, tried to even the account by the use of school funds. He could not do it, and departed suddenly for Iowa about $600 short, it is claimed. He sent his family ahead of him, and left all mortgaged property.

The eight Italians charged with the murder of Charles T. Hubbard at Hawthorne, Wis., about three weeks ago have been bound over to be tried by the grand jury at the spring term of court. It is now reported that only three of them took part in the killing, and that the remaining five were forced to run by their belief that they would be mobbed if captured.

Edward Goetzinger, a young man employed by the bottling works at Helena, Montana, was arrested on a requisition from Gov. Thayer of Nebraska, on the charge of embezzling $150 in that state. He started for Lincoln in charge of the deputy sheriff of Colfax county, Neb. Goetzinger has been in Helena only a short time, and since the campaign opened has made himself prominent by speeches for the Democrats at meetings of the German Democratic club.

Information received at Omaha states that 21 Union Pacific brakemen and conductors have been indicted at Rawlins, Wyo., for robbing freight trains. Their stealings run up into the thousands, being confined wholly to through cars. Four of them are now under arrest. The matter was discovered by one of the thieves, he having made a full confession in consideration of immunity form punishment. The others will be under arrest in a few days, Prominent business men in Rawlins are also implicated. The thieving was carried on between Rawlins and Green River.

W. L. Morrison, a former county official of Barron, Wis., has been placed in the jail after leading the sheriff an eventful chase. Morrison about four years ago suddenly disappeared after a sharp business transaction. He was subsequently arrested, but settled the affair and lived with his family apparently a good citizen. About a year ago he eloped with a married woman, leaving his family destitute. Last spring he was discovered to be in Missouri. The sheriff of Barron left at once and secured Morrison. On the return trip Morrison leaped from the rapidly moving train and escaped. All efforts to find him failed, until a few days ago he was arrested in Wisconsin, and will be tried for adultery.

Pauline McCoy, a negro girl aged nineteen, was hanged at Union Springs, Ala., for the murder of Annie Jordan, a fourteen-year-old white child, last February. The execution was private, only the necessary persons being admitted. The crime for which the woman was hanged was a peculiar one. The victim, Annie Jordan, strayed away from her home in Montgomery and was not heard from till her dead body was found in a plumb thicket at Three Notch. Circumstances pointed to Pauline, and she was arrested with the dead girl's clothing on her. She was found guilty last spring and sentenced to death. Efforts were made to have the governor intercede, but to no avail.

A fatal saloon row occurred at the close o the monthly fair at Cokato, Minn., James Erickson, a saloon keeper of Annandale, was in one of the saloons, and had some words with those present. About this time John Anderson, a well-known farmer of French Lake township, entered the same saloon in an inebriated condition, and entered into a dispute with the bartender as to the price of some drinks. Erickson chimed in and made some insulting remarks to Anderson. Upon the latter's telling him not to address him in such a tone of voice, Erickson struck Anderson two powerful blows, one in the neck and the other in the stomach, killing him almost instantly. Erickson was at once arrested, and is now in Buffalo in the custody of Sheriff Nugent.

Thomas Wardell a very wealthy land owner and coal operator, was shot and instantly killed by a number of striking miners. Mr. Wardell had driven from Macon in his carriage, accompanied only by a colored boy. He stopped his horses at Berier, Mo., and crossed the railroad track, going into the telegraphic office to send a message. The depot platform was filled with striking miners, and as he passed through the crowd, going to his carriage, they jeered and taunted him. Turning, he said: "Boys, I'll beat you in the end; you can holler all you want." The men commenced throwing stones at him, and he was struck in the back by one. Upon reaching his carriage Mr. Wardell took from under the seat a large revolver and fired one shot in the direction of the crowd, but above their heads. In an instant a half dozen shots or more came from the crowd, and Wardell dropped lifeless.

A FIEND STRANGLED.
Summary Punishment of a Negro Rapist at Tiptonville.
Summary Punishment of a Negro Rapist at Tiptonville.

Information reached the city yesterday of the summary disposal of a brutal negro fiend at Tiptonville, Lake county, on Wednesday morning. The account is as follows:

On Saturday last information was given to the authorities that Jerry Smith, a colored man, had attempted to rape a white girl aged about twelve years, and the daughter of a farmer residing about three miles from Tiptonville. The constable went in search of the scoundrel, and after a race through the overflowed bottoms, during which both stood a good chance of being drowned, succeeded in capturing him and placed him in jail.

Wednesday was court day at Tiptonville, and the prisoner was to be tried, but Judge Lynch arrived in town just before daybreak. The impromptu jurist convened his court, tried, convicted and executed the culprit before the legitimate tribunal was called to order. The body of the lascivious negro was seen yesterday morning, about a quarter of a mile back from the bank of the river, suspended from a tree. As is usual with Judge Lynch and his followers, their work was done without leaving a trace of their identity.

On Tuesday night last a shooting affray occurred at the house kept by some colored women by the name of Cooper, in East Hickman, near the colored Methodist church, in which Henry Prather was shot and it is thought fatally wounded, and also Amos Nichols received two painful wounds in the leg. One report says that the men were gambling, and that the fight originated about the game, and another report has it that it was about the women. Perhaps both causes had somewhat to do with its origination. Alec Cooper, who it is said, did all the shooting, is a brother of the Cooper women who keep the house, and Henry Montgomery, who is in some way implicated, but did no shooting, is his brother-in-law. If arrests are made, the facts will be brought out.

Henry Prather, after great suffering, died, Thursday morning, from the effects of his wounds.

At 11 o'clock last night there was nothing unusual to break the solitude of the place. MICCOSUKIE'S RED CRIME
ONE OF THE MURDERERS A SON OF
MRS. MARY E. BRYAN.
MONTICELLO, FLA., Nov. 23. — Interest in a horrible murder that occurred near here recently has been intensified by the discovery that one of the men implicated is a son of Mary E. Bryan, the well-known writer of New York. Mrs. Bryan was in this city last week to look after her son's interests, and left a day or two ago for Thomasville, Ga., where it is supposed she is still stopping. The story she told is a pathetic one. Just before the election she received a letter urging her to come to Florida, as her son was taking a very active part in politics and it was feared that he would get into trouble with the negroes at the polls at Lloyd's, Jefferson county, where he voted. Her next summons was a dispatch which read: "Come at once." When she arrived, she learned that her son was a fugitive, with a suspicion of murder hanging over him. This unexpected announcement was a terrible blow, but she at once put her son's interests in the hands of a lawyer, who has advised that he surrender and stand trial. Mrs. Bryan knows his whereabouts, but whether she has had a personal interview with him yet is not certain. The story of his crime is tragic in the extreme. In a fracas in a mill at Lloyd's station a month ago he was stabbed, and at one time his life was despaired of. Who cut him was uncertain, but a negro named Judson Cason was suspected. On election day Lee Houston, John L. Bryan, son of the authoress, and Arthur Duncan arrested Judson. That night he was taken from a room in which he was confined at Lloyds, bound hand and foot, placed in a wagon and carried two miles to the Miccosukie sinks. There he was stabbed to death, at least a dozen ghastly wounds being inflicted. Five or six heavy stones were then tied to the body, and it was thrown into the yawning abyss forming the mouth of the sinks. Had it not struck an obstruction it would have disappeared in the fathomless opening and never been found. It struck on a ledge, however, was discovered next morning, and thus brought out the story of the crime. The coroner's jury brought in a verdict charging six men with complicity. Of these, only one was captured. The grand jury indicted Bryan, Houston, Duncan and Gus Simmons. The others turned state's evidence, and are free. In speaking of her son, Mrs. Bryan said that she was only 15 years old when he was born, and that he had been separated from her when very young, and thus grew up without the restraint of a mother's influence. Bryan is said to be still suffering from the wound inflicted in the fracas in the mill. Whether he will surrender is unknown.

MRS. BRYAN INTERVIEWED.

The editor of the Monticello Constitution had an interview with Mrs. Bryan a day or two ago.

"What do you suppose ever induced the men to commit the crime?" he asked her.

She replied: "My son thought this negro was the one who stabbed him at the mill, and as he (J. L. B.) had spent some time in the states of Louisiana and Arkansas, where six men constitute a court, I assure you that my son thought he was doing perfectly right when they killed the negro."

"Mrs. Bryan, how do you account for your son's reckless disposition?" inquired the editor.

"He was born before I was 15 years old, and separated from me; he never knew what a mother's influence was, he grew up without any restraint whatever, and being very ambitious, and having no opportunities, and not knowing what fear was, he has become very reckless, but at heart a better man never lived."

Mrs. Bryan told a great deal about her former life, her trials in Louisiana just after the war, when she was editing a political paper, and had to carry a pistol in a belt around her waist for self-protection against the republicans; and of her accumulations for years, derived from the sale of her books, which she had deposited in James' bank of Atlanta, and which failed, but she affirmed that of all her trials and troubles, the present was the greatest.

"Did you see your son when you arrived at his home?" asked the Constitution scribe.

"I did not. When I reached his home he was not there."

"Do you know where he has gone?"

"Oh, yes; he is only a short distance from home; but as there had been so much rain during the past few days the water was so high that it was impossible for me to get to him."

"There is a report in Monticello that he is very sick and not expected to live. Can you inform me of his true condition?" asked
"He is now suffering from the wound which he received in the mill a few weeks ago, but it is feared that blood poison has set in, and I am very uneasy about his condition."

"Does your son intend giving himself up to the authorities and stand a trial for the crime of which he is charged?"

"So soon as he is in a condition to stand the confinement in prison he will surrender himself to the authorities, but in his present feeble condition the confinement would surely kill him."

An Indian Scare Among Settlers Near Flathead Lake.

HELENA March 27th A few days ago
An Indian Scare Among Settlers Near Flathead Lake.

HELENA, March 27th.—A few days ago word was received that the settlers north of Flathead lake had discovered the murderers of the three white men, committed last summer by Kootenai Indians, and had armed themselves to go in search of and punish the murderers. It would seem that they had accomplished their purpose, for a letter containing the following extract was received from a resident of that section Saturday.

"Here we are, all up at G. M. Lakins on account of the Kootenai scare. All of the families from Elliott's down, except Henry Bartlett's are here. Those above Elliott's, on this side, have gone to the Sheldon school-house. Those on the east side have retired to Ashley.

"The trouble arose from the lynching of two Indian murderers at Penny's mill. Though nothing definite has been learned it is understood that the Kootenais have taken the warpath.

"A squad of men from Selish are guarding the point of rocks. Another of our party are defending Lee's ferry and we are seeing to the Big Fork's ford. Don't be worried, for we don't anticipate serious trouble."

Nothing has been heard from that section since then, and it is presumed there has been no active hostilities.

Some weeks ago a warrant for the arrest of two Kootenai Indians was sworn out in the justice's court at Ashley, Montana. The Indians were arrested and placed in charge of a deputy sheriff. During the deputy's absence a party of citizens, numbering fifty or sixty, overpowered the guard, took the prisoners to the east side of the river, and, it is supposed, "made good Indians" of them. The crime charged against them was murder. It is alleged that these Indians assisted a third Kootenai in killing three prospectors on Wolf Creek last June. Two of these men were well along in years, and the third was a young man. After shooting them, it is claimed they were beaten over the head with six-shooters until life was extinct, and their bodies were then burned. It is asserted by responsible men that the above named "Mood Indians" confessed complicity in the fearful crime and made an open boast of their prowess. The booty received was $6 in money, a scanty supply of provisions and two ponies. The ponies, it is claimed, are now in the possession of the fugitive Indians. A company of fifty white men made a peaceful visit to Dayton Creek and had a talk with Chief Aenas, of the Kootenais, resulting, as claimed, in an agreement between the whites and Indians to bury the hatchet, Chief Aenas agreeing to turn over the fugitive Indian to the legal authority if caught. A correspondent writing from Thompson Falls gives the following account of the beginning of the trouble: "The first of July, 1887, Ben Thompkins, one Johnson and Daniel McDonald left Libby with two pack animals to prospect in the Kootenais. They never have been heard of since. There is considerable mail at Goodchild & Co.'s of this place for McDonald. Every one in this part is satisfied that they are the parties murdered."
penny-s-mill-penny-s-mill.A10:
HI YU SKOOKUM!
Two of the Three Kootenai Murderers
Hanged to a Tree.
A gentleman who came in from Flathead Lake Friday gave the Missoulian a vivid description of the recent stirring events in that section of Missoula county. Everything has assumed its usual quiet, and once more peace reigns supreme in Flathead valley.

The plans of the settlers to capture the three Kootenai Indians who murdered three prospectors on Wolf creek in June or July last were well laid out. Between forty-five and fifty of them gathered at Demersville early in the morning and proceeded in a body to the Indian lodges, located between one and two miles below town. The lodges were reached while the Indians were still sleeping soundly. One lodge after another was searched, and guards left to prevent an outtery or voice of warning, until the lodge where two of the murderers were sleeping was found. The names of these two Kootenais were John Ninna and Slume. They were forcibly taken by the settlers, who were all armed and determined to carry out their plans at all hazards.

The name of the third murderer was Antley. Antley was not there; he was in Smith's valley, several miles distant. As soon as the settlers left with their prisoners an Indian jumped upon the fleet st horse in the camp and dashed wildly away to Smith's valley. He went to warn Antley of the danger, and his mission was successful. The fugitive was notified and he fled in haste, probably toward the British possessions. It is stated that the settlers of Smith's valley had promised to arrest Antley, but they failed to do so, and he is probably forever safe from the reach of the vengeance of the people of Flathead Lake.

Ninna and Slume were taken to Demersville. A hasty consultation was had when the two murderers were hastened to the river bank, a skiff was procured, the savages were rowed across the river, never to return. The settlers acted cautiously, quietly, but determinedly. They resolved to hang the two Indians, instead of turning them over to the law and its uncertain results. The murderers were informed that they were going to be hung, and one of them defiantly retorted, "Hi yu Skookum," which means powerful good. It is said they made no attempt to conceal the murder of the prospectors, but even bragged of their savage instinct and of making the white man's flesh smoke and quiver in the flames.

They were taken into the woods lining the east bank of the Flathead river at that place, ropes were fastened about their necks and they were swung up to the limb of a tree. A short time afterwards the bodies were cut down and buried.

After this stirring event considerable excitement prevailed both among the whites and Indians. The latter packed up their duds and fled to the Arm of the Lake. Subsequently a report spread among the settlers of danger, when they organized a large company and, thoroughly armed, went down to interview the chief, Aeneas. When the Arm of the Lake was reached the Indians mixed in with the whites and acted in a defiant and warlike manner. Aeneas was on the road to the mission and a courier was sent after him with all haste. He was overtaken and induced to return, when a consultation was had, resulting in an amicable understanding. The settlers then returned to their homes, feeling much relief.

Nina, Slume and Antley were bad Indians, and the death of the two former occasioned little if any mourning. At latest accounts both the whites and Indians were entirely satisfied, and there is no danger of further trouble between them, so far as the muders are concerned.

From the Daily Herald of April 14. THE KOOTENAI TROUBLE. No Serious Disturbance Nor Any Future Danger Apprehended.
SHELDON, Mont., April 11.—TO THE EDITOR OF THE HERALD:—In your issue of the 29th of last month there was a short communication from one of the besieged at Fort Lakin. Although, the article was written in apparent good faith, the writer was undoubtedly laboring under the impression that the reported hostile demonstration of the Kootenais was true. For the sake of the public I will here state that there never was at any time before or immediately after the lynching any danger of an outbreak.

There were only two or three Indians, and those near relations, of the deceased, that expressed any hostile intentions, and their threats were directed against those prominent in the lynching. Even this was regarded by the persons as only bragadocia and no fear was ever entertained of any danger.

The relations of the Kootenais as a tribe have ever been friendly towards the whites, and it has only been the knife of the assassin instead of the war hatchet of the plumed warrior to be feared.

Nothing, perhaps, could assure the public of the utter absurdity of an outbreak so well as the disparity in the number of Indians and whites. At the arm of the lake from whence the danger was expected there were at the time not to exceed thirty-five warriors, and scarcely one-half of them had guns and a great many no ammunition, and to oppose this half-starved mob of red striplings and superannuated braves, there was nearly if not quite 400 white men in this vicinity with a rifle and ammunition in every home.

In the pow-wow with the chief, which immediately followed the alarm so diligently spread by a few excited people, he expressed himself satisfied with the hanging of the murderers, and further agreed to give up the remaining one in case he was apprehended. The opinion of the thinking people of Flathead and those well able to form a verdict, is that we are in less danger to-day than before, not only from any serious trouble, but from all those petty grievances which the whites have so long suffered at the hands of the Kootenai renegades allowed free access to their homes. And if the Indian department continues in the future as in the past to utterly disregard the interests and rights of pioneer settlers in relation to the Indians, there is a strong feeling among settlers here that they will exact an obedience to law and order from the red men which the indifference and neglect of organized law has failed to secure. In his report to Maj. Gen. Ruger on the recent trouble between the Kootenai Indians and the settlers near Ashley, Agent Renan says:

It is a fact that the citizens of that vicinity did execute two Kootenai Indians some time last month, and that a third one made his escape or he would have followed the fate of the other two. From diligent inquiries among the Indians of this reservation, I am afraid that the reported murder of three white men is true, and that no mistake is made by the citizens as to the identity of the Indian murderers. The white men were killed about the 17th of last June, at a place called Wolf Creek, on the trail leading to Tobacco plains. The Indians who committed the crime, and who were lynched, are said to belong to the bandit Chief Eneas, who have their homes on the reservation, and live about six miles north of the agency at Dayton creek. One of the murderers, who is still at large, confessed the crime to reliable Indians of this reserve. It seems that a party of some ten Kootenai Indians, while passing along the trail, noticed three white men encamped. One Indian proposed to two others to go to the camp and intimidate the whites. On nearing them the Indians fired over their heads, but the white men only laughed; whereupon the Indians decided to kill them. Two of the white party being seated eating in range, a bullet fired by an Indian passed through both men, killing them instantly. The third was fired upon and wounded, and was killed by the blows of an ax. No motive was given for the crime. I sent for Chief Eneas, of the reservation Kootenais, and he told me he had met a party of white men at Dayton creek. Their leader, one Ramsdale, told him they had hung two of his Indians, and were there to find out what he was going to do about it. It was explained to Eneas that a white traveler who had camped near Dayton creek, on hearing of the hanging of the Indians, mounted a horse and rode into Ashley and stated that the band of Eneas' were in arms; that they had attacked him, and he made his escape while the Indians were plundering his wagon. This was easily refuted by Eneas. The action of the white man who caused the excitement at the reservation is inexcusable. Chief Eneas, in his talk to me, stated that if murder had been committed by the Indians, it was nothing more than justice to hang the guilty ones, but was sorry that the lake settlers took the law into their own hands and lynched the prisoners, as a trial, conviction and execution by due process of law would have a more salutary effect upon the Indians and prevent recourse to revenge. COLUMBIA, Dec. 20.—The recent race trouble in Barnwell county, in this State, has had a very funny ending. The story, as originally told, was that Robert Morris, a farmer, had been kidnapped and murdered by negroes. The usual armed posse of whites was organized and scoured the swamps in search of the body of the victim, and also to avenge his murder. The poor negroes became frightened and hid out. Morris's overcoat and gun were found in the woods, and the excitement became intense. Last night the hunters and avengers found Morris dead drunk in the woods and the story leaked out.

It seems that the Morris family got their Christmas jug of whiskey earlier than they expected. Barnwell is what is called a dry county. No liquor is sold there except in jugs and demi-johns. The whole party got drunk, and Robert Morris, with an attack of jim-jams on him, saw not snakes and rats, but niggers and shotguns, which is a peculiarity of the jim-jams in certain counties in this State. They started out armed in search of the guns and niggers, and, taking the jug with them, got lost in the woods, where they lynched imaginary niggers for two nights and a day, while their neighbors were searching for their corpses and their murderers. The people of Bamberg have returned to their watermelon fields very much incensed.

THE FIFTIETH CONGRESS.

The Benet Circular in the Senate—Democratic Hypocrisy About Public Lands.

WASHINGTON, Oct. 1.—Mr. Plumb, from the committee on public lands, reported the Senate bill for the disposal of Fort Wallace military reservation, in Kansas, and asked for its immediate consideration, stating that a bill on the same subject had passed both houses at this session and had been vetoed by the President, whose objections, he said, were unimportant, but the bill had been amended so as to cover these objections.

Mr. Edmunds objected to its present consideration, and it was placed on the calendar. Later in the day the bill was, however, passed.

The President's message to Congress announcing his approval of the Chinese exclusion bill was laid before the Senate and read.

Mr. Sherman moved that it be printed and referred to the committee on foreign relations. He remarked that the only legislative suggestion made in it had already been acted on—an appropriation of $276,000 having been put in the deficiency bill to indemnify Chinese for losses inflicted on them in the territories.

Mr. Hale remarked that that item was now in conference between the two houses.

Mr. Dolph suggested that that was not the only matter suggested for legislation in the message. It also recommended immediate legislation to authorize the landing of Chinese laborers now on their way with certificates. He regarded it as a very extraordinary proposition for the President to approve a bill cutting off summarily and completely the entrance of Chinese, and then ask Congress to disapprove of it and to amend it.

The message was referred to the committee on foreign relations.

Mr. Hale offered a resolution reciting the circular of Gen. Benet directing the discharge of Republican employees from the United States arsenals, stating that under it honorably discharged soldiers of the Union army, and widows and daughters of soldiers, have been discharged, and directing the Secretary of War to transmit to the Senate forthwith full information as to such order, stating fully whether the necessities of the department required that the order should be issued, and why an order issued on public business should be marked "confidential."

Mr. Hale remarked that there was nothing in the previous history or record of the Secretary of War that would have led him (Mr. Hale) to believe that he would have permitted or authoritarianized the issuing of such a circular, extending (for the first time) party proscription to women and children. He did not know in the history of party politics and party conflicts an instance where the dogma "To the Victors Belong the Spoils" had been carried to that extent.

Mr. Cockrell objected to immediate consideration of the resolution, and said that he, to-morrow, would fully answer the remarks of the Senator from Maine, and would state what the Democratic party was responsible for, what it was not responsible for, and what it should have done long ago. The resolution went over till to-morrow.

The Senate then took up, as unfinished business, the Senate bill reported from the committee on public lands on August 30, restoring to the United States certain of the lands granted to the Northern Pacific Railroad Company, and was addressed by Mr. Berry. He contrasted the position of the Democratic House of Representatives and of the Republican Senate on railroad land forfeitures, and claimed that, while the bill which passed the Senate this session only forfeited between 5,000,000 and 6,000,000 acres, the amendment to it adopted by the House, and which was now in conference between the two houses, forfeited 36,000,000 acres.

In no part of the record of the Republican party, he said, had it been more clearly shown that it was a friend of corporations and not of the people than in its dealings with the public lands.

Mr. Plum said the House of Representatives was not the Democratic party. The President of the United States was the Democratic party, and the President himself had patented more than 700,000 acres to the railroad companies, which lands were earned years and years after the time limited in the law. He [Mr. Plumb] would prophesy that between election day and the day when Congress would next assemble, another large lot of land would be patented to another railroad company (earned out of time)—a railroad company, the president of which was one of the largest contributors to the Democratic campaign fund. On motion of Mr. Dolph, the House bill on the same subject was substituted for the Senate bill, and then Mr. Dolph offered the Senate bill as a substitute for the House bill, the object and effect being the passage of the House bill with an amendment. A Chester Constable and his Prisoner Fired Upon from an Ambush-The Prisoner Killed.
[Special to the World.]
CHESTER, Sept. 29.—Reports reached here this morning of the murder of a negro on the public road about eight miles from this place. About 4 o'clock this morning twelve or fifteen pistol shots were heard by parties living at some distance from the road, then the sounds of three or four horses moving rapidly. Shortly after daylight a gentleman was driving to town, and saw the body of a negro man laying across the road with his hands tied together and about twelve bullet holes in his body.

Later in the day the following particulars of the tragedy were learned:

T. W. Lippford had Sam Cornwall, a negro, under arrest on a peace warrant, and was on his way to a trial justice, with an extra guard of three men. About 4 o'clock they were fired into from an ambush. The constable and others fled, and Sam Cornwall was instantly killed.

On an examination by Dr. Davega fifteen bullet holes were found in the body. At the coroner's inquest the evidence was that Sam Cornwall came to his death by gun-shot wounds inflicted by parties unknown to the constable and others.

No arrests have been made. Further investigation will be pushed by Coroner Murphy. A 45-calibre Winchester rifle was used.

Sensational Lawsuit at Greensburg.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

GREENSBURG, Sept. 19.—A suit that will attract much attention was filed in the Circuit Court to-day. The title is Mary J. Vornholt vs. Sarah R. Roberts and Wm. R. Roberts. The facts connected with it are these: Jeremiah K. Tullis and wife lived near Sardinia, this county, many years ago, and became quite wealthy. Their only child was the plaintiff in this action, now Mary J. Vornholt, her husband being a merchant at Westport. About five years ago the mother died, and soon after the father threw off the habiliments of mourning, and became gay and festive for one of his age—about sixty-five years. He went to Indianapolis to live with the defendants, Mrs. Roberts being quite attractive, and much younger than Mr. Tullis. Oct. 22, 1866, Tullis made a deed to Mrs. Roberts for 160 acres of fine farming land, on which he and his wife formerly lived, retaining, however, to himself a life estate. The consideration, as expressed in the deed, was "For the sum and consideration of my support heretofore and hereafter, and of natural love and affection, the receipt whereof is hereby acknowledged." Mr. Tullis died a few days ago, and Mrs. Roberts now has possession of the land. This suit by the daughter is for the recovery of the farm and damages. There will probably be another action in Marion county, as he also gave her a deed for a house and lot in Indianapolis which he owned. Mrs. Roberts is not a relative in any way of Mr. Tullis, but formerly lived at Lebanon, Ind.

GERTRUDE DOWNEY'S MURDERER.
A Knox County Jurr Says Sylvester Grubb Must Suffer the Extreme Penalty.
VINCENNES, Ind., Oct. 19.—The trial of Sylvester Grubb for the murder of Miss Gertrude Downey was begun in the Knox Circuit Court Oct. 12. The defense was a plea of insanity, and a strong pull was made to save his neck from the rope. The case was a romance-tragedy in real life, and excited great interest in this community, the court-room being crowded day after day to hear the shocking details of the story.

Grubb is a young man, twenty-four years of age, and two years ago met Miss Gertie Downey. It was a case of love at first sight. Both these young people lived in Gibson county. Letters passed between them, and then Grubb proposed marriage. The young lady did not wish to marry him, and refused longer to see him. Then he wrote her a letter, vowing revenge, if she cast him off forever. He proposed to go away for a year, and see how that would do. He told her he would disgrace her forever if she cast him off. This letter was introduced in the trial. A day or two before the tragedy he called at her home at Francisco, eight miles east of Princeton, and when the young lady refused to see him he sat for three hours on a pile of lumber near the house, hoping still to have the privilege of seeing her, but all in vain. On the morning of the fatal 13th of September he went to the Princeton fair, hoping to see her there. On the way he remarked to a friend that she was there with another young man, and he wanted to see her but once more. They met on the fair ground, and he asked her to walk with him. Unwillingly she went with him, telling her lady friend to remain at that spot, as she would be back in a few minutes. As they went toward an unfrequented part of the ground, it was observed that they were quarreling. Suddenly, and without notice, he shoved his revolver in her face and fired, the ball striking just below the right eye, and the powder burning her face. She turned and ran away screaming, the blood saturating her white dress. He fired two other shots at her, one hitting her in the arm, the other missing its mark. Then he pointed the pistol at his own head, and snapped it twice, but it failed to go off. When parties rushed in to interfere, he flourished his revolver around and told them to stand back. After a moment, however, he surrendered to the officers, and was at once lodged in jail.

The young lady died in great agony, after lingering six days, and the indignation of Miss Downey's friends was so great that an attempt was made to lynch the murderer. His neck was saved by spiriting him away to Evansville. Then he was taken to Jeffersonville for safe keeping, and was brought here for trial.

The jury took the case last evening. On the first ballot the jury decided that Grubb was guilty of murder in the first degree. The second ballot was to decide whether it should be the death penalty or imprisonment for life, and nine were for inflicting the extreme penalty of the law. The insanity dodge was not considered in the jury-room at all. After deliberating eight hours a verdict of death was reached.

The prisoner was brought into court this morning and the sentence read to him. He seemed to take it as a matter of course, and there was scarcely a perceptible blanch on his cheek. Many encomiums have been passed upon the jury for its moral courage in affixing the death penalty as a matter of justice to the slain girl.

A NEGRO MUTILILATED, HUNG TO A
TREE AND THEN SHOT.
The Avenging Accomplished at the County Seat of Colquitt in Broad Daylight Without Masks—Some of the Most Prominent Citizens in the County Said to Have Taken a Hand. BAINBRIDGE, GA., Sept. 5.—In December last a negro named Thomas Reese, alias Samuel Long, for two years previous living with William Reagan of Miller county outraged Mrs. Reagan and afterward attempted to kill her with strychnine to conceal his crime, and then effected his escape. Nothing could be learned of his whereabouts until two weeks ago, when a neighbor of Mr. Reagan discovered him in Randolph county, Ala., and on Saturday effected his capture in Eufaula, whence he was brought to Moultrie, Colquitt county, on Monday night last and lodged in jail.

TERRIBLE VENGEANCE.

His capture aroused the citizens of Mitchell county as probably they never were aroused before, and terrible and swift justice was soon upon the demon. The news of his capture spread like wildfire, and on Tuesday afternoon several hundred men had congregated in the village. Four o'clock in the afternoon had been named as the time for his trial before a committing court. The trial was held as arranged. The prisoner had been questioned and had freely admitted his guilt before the trial, but the crowd deemed it best to let the law develop the first facts. After the hearing he was ordered committed, but instead the crowd, in broad daylight and without mask or disguise, took him to the edge of an adjacent swamp, and placing a rope around his neck prepared to take his life.

A HORRIBLE MUTILATION.

Before doing so, however, a very unusual and terrible surgical operation was performed, as a warning to others of his class and race. The crowd then suspended his body to a convenient limb, and after riddling it with bullet holes, left it as food for the buzzards. It was, however, subsequently cut down and buried. A hundred or more men had a hand in the affair. Among the number were some of the most prominent citizens of Miller county. These people are opposed to mob law, but in this case under the circumstances they do not feel that they are to blame, first having made themselves absolutely certain of the identity of the criminal and of his crime as detailed.

WILKESBARRE, June 17.—James Cobley, a local prize fighter, and William Parry, a miner, got into an altercation at Cranberry to-day. Parry said when it came to a day's work in the mines he was a better man than Cobley, although probably the latter was a better man when it came to prize fighting. Wood's Holl, Mass., June 17.—A Fish Commission has left here with live lobsters for stocking the Pacific coast waters in the region about San Francisco. The shipment consists of over 600 lobsters, a large proportion being females, many of which are now carrying eggs nearly ready to hatch. In addition a lot of 200,000 free eggs, arranged on cloth trays, is also included in the shipment, and these will be hatched artificially after their arrival in San Francisco.
